root_cause.text: `__smc_setsockopt()` in the SMC socket option handler performed a potentially blocking `copy_from_sockptr()` while holding `lock_sock(sk)`, allowing a user-controlled page fault to sleep inside the socket lock and stall other kernel work.
root_cause.evidence: The patch explicitly says it fixes “sleep-inside-lock in `__smc_setsockopt()`,” moves the `copy_from_sockptr(&val, optval, sizeof(int))` and length check outside `lock_sock(sk)`, and the CVE description notes an attacker can use a userfaultfd/FUSE-backed `optval` to keep the lock held indefinitely, blocking `smc_shutdown()` and triggering hung tasks.

intent_record.intent_summary: Move user-option validation and copying outside the socket lock for SMC_LIMIT_HS to shorten the locked section without changing behavior.
intent_record.what: The `SMC_LIMIT_HS` handling was moved out of the `lock_sock(sk)` critical section: the code now checks `optlen` and copies `optval` into `val` before acquiring the socket lock, and the redundant validation/copy block was removed from inside the `switch` case. The assignment to `smc->limit_smc_hs` remains under the lock.
intent_record.how: Runtime behavior is unchanged for valid and invalid inputs, but the socket lock is held for less time because the potentially blocking user-memory access happens before locking. This reduces lock contention and avoids performing user copies while the socket is locked.

grouping_result.intent: Move user-option validation and copying outside the socket lock for SMC_LIMIT_HS to shorten the locked section without changing behavior.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it moves the user-controlled copy/validation out of the locked section, avoiding a potentially blocking copy_from_sockptr() under lock_sock(sk) in __smc_setsockopt().

candidates.rationale: This acquires the socket lock before the option handling logic, and the vulnerable copy_from_sockptr() occurs while this lock is held, enabling a potentially sleeping page fault inside the critical section.
This is the blocking user-memory copy that can fault/sleep while the socket lock is held, directly matching the root cause.

vuln_statements.explanation: This user-memory copy was executed inside __smc_setsockopt() while lock_sock(sk) was already held, so a page fault in copy_from_sockptr() could sleep within the socket lock and stall other kernel work, matching the root cause.
This acquires the socket lock before the option-copying logic, creating the critical section in which the blocking copy_from_sockptr() was performed and making the sleep-in-lock bug possible.

Author: Ursula Braun <ubraun@linux.ibm.com>

    net/smc: handle sockopts forcing fallback
    
    Several TCP sockopts do not work for SMC. One example are the

    If the SMC socket is still in state SMC_INIT, such sockopts trigger

bic_trace_step.reason: The vulnerable construct described in the root cause is a potentially blocking `copy_from_sockptr()` performed while holding `lock_sock(sk)` inside `__smc_setsockopt()`. The shown `smc_setsockopt()` function does not perform any `copy_from_sockptr()` itself; it first calls the underlying CLC socket `setsockopt()` (`rc = smc->clcsock->ops->setsockopt(...)`), and only after that, if `rc == 0`, it takes `lock_sock(sk)` and handles only local state changes in the `switch (optname)` block. The critical blocking copy is absent from this snippet, so the vulnerable construct is not present here. Additionally, this code already avoids doing the underlying socket option call under `lock_sock(sk)`; the lock is acquired only after the call returns, which is the correct mitigation for the described issue.
